blocks.x: Let's see, first thing we want is your name in here.
My name is Avery Kidd Howard.
Avery Kidd Howard, huh? That's right. And uh, let's see, what's today's date?
May the 22nd.

1961. That's right. Yeah, and this is the first reel, and uh, we're at Tulane University. Room, Seminar Room 2, Howard Tilton Library. Fine, good. All right. Uh, we ought to start at the beginning, huh? Why not? That's a good place to start.
Can I help please?
Yeah. Uh, I better put my name on him, too, and his. What's your name real loud?
Andrew Stewart.
And my name is uh, Dick Allen. Okay, let's see, uh, maybe we can ask you when you were born.
I was born 1908, uh, April the 22nd.
And where? In New Orleans. Exactly what street? Do you know?
Well, I think it was Boybin Street. Yeah. Near what? Near uh, St. Claude. Now Paul, though.
No, it was Boybin at that time. Yeah, but now Paul, though. It's Paul, but that's right. Now. So, uh, did you grow up here in the city?
Uh, well, uh, say from 12 years up. I was at Phoenix, Louisiana. Uh, at the age around of five years old up until 12 years old. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
Do you remember anything, uh, before you were five of the city?
Well, no, not exactly. I was in and out, but I don't remember nothing particularly. Nothing about, uh, the music or anything you heard?
Not at that time. Yeah, too young.
About 12 years, and I knew it. Uh-huh, I see.
Well, what about your music out in Phoenix, Louisiana?
Well, I wasn't into, I mean, I was too young for that at that time. I got interested in it when I had to come back to the city.
Did you hear any music out there?
Well, no, I wouldn't see nothing but guitars, something like that.
Who played guitars out there?
Well, all the fellas. Mostly blues. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Do you remember any blues they played out there? Just the regular blues.
Twelve bar, eight bar, right? Or what?
Oh, something about a twelve bar, eight bar, something like that. Old standard blues.
Standard blues, that's all. I got the picture now. Yeah.
Did you go to church out there? Oh, yeah, I did.
I went to church, Sunday schools every Sunday.
Uh-huh. What did you sing in Sunday school? Well, mostly, uh, Near On My God, The Deans Soap, with a friend we have to sing.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Did they have any instruments in the church?
No, not at that time. None at all?
No, no, nothing at all. The grown up people didn't even have that? No, they just sing.
The choir didn't have any music in the background.
Uh-huh. Do you remember what the grown people sang?
Well, most of them like they sing in the choir of these days.
About the same thing?
Yeah. They just turn the song, you know, raise the tempo, you may say, on the songs, faster. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Uh-huh. What church was that? St. John's Baptist Church. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh.
The city? Well, when you came to the city, was it any different in music there?

Well, when I came to the city I started working on Connell Street as a porter and a curio store and I was very much interested all my life about music and that's how it started. Around the age of about 14 I played drums.
You were working in what kind of store? A curio store.
Curio store where they sold alligators, different little- Oh yeah, curio.
Yeah, curio, that's right. I see. Right next to Waylines. They didn't have any music in there, huh? In the store, never.
No, right next to Waylines, there was music there. Yeah.
Did they have live bands in Waylines then?
No, they had them on the streets, I mean parades and the advertising, bands on the trucks.
Uh-huh. I just wondered, because you hear about music in department stores, you know, did you ever hear any of that when the bands would go in department stores and play?
No, I don't remember that.
Somebody told me about it, I guess it was one of the older fellas.
It could have been.
That he used to go in the store and they'd have a band up on the second floor playing for the public.
Well I know different clothes in stores on Ramport and St. Charles so far, and different fellas used to play on the balcony.
Oh yeah?

During that time. Sam Morgan, he played at Mise en Blanche in the stores, then he used to play on the truck, which I took part of it later on in the years, you know? Played on the truck, advertised for Mise en Blanche, and it.
Do you remember who played with Manuel Perez in those years? I don't know why I just know them. Who played with Sam Morgan then?
Well, Big Jim, Little Jim, Johnny Deve, Alfred Williams. Well they didn't have, Oilo Fusje, Andrew Morgan. How about eight men?
Did he have a second car now?
That's right, Young Morgan, his brother. Isil Morgan.
Which is Big Jim? Big Jim? Yeah, who is he?
Jim Robinson. I wanted you to tell me. Jim Robinson.
And Little Jim we know who that is. Sidney Brown. Did they have a piano in those kind of jobs?
Not at that particular time. They wasn't using any.
So when they'd play, I guess they wouldn't have a piano in the department stores up there on those balconies?
No, they wouldn't have it.
Let's see. Did you have a teacher when you first got started?
Oh, when I first started, my first lesson, I went to Chris Kelly. And from-
You mean on drums now?

On drums? No. Well that was something that went about that I said I couldn't play, which I couldn't. I did many times go to parties. And so finally one night, Young Morgan's band, he had his on band at that particular time, and I went to a party and the drummer got hooked. And so when I walked in, they said, well here come a drummer. Well I couldn't get up and I went up and played with him. Jim Robinson was with Young Morgan at that particular time. And then Andrew Morgan came in and they liked what I was doing and they hired me, which I didn't have a drum. I didn't even know how to put them up. I went to Weller, I asked the following, then bought a drum for, set a drum for $62.50. And Dr. Bache was playing trombone, Sonny's Year on trumpet, and Morgan on the clarinet, a fellow called Bouton, Bays. Called what?
Bouton.
Bouton.
Yeah. Like button in French. Yeah. I like that.
Yeah. I just remember the rest of the fellow, there were about six of us anyway. And I started playing the drum with them and then with Chris, you know, job around with different fellows.
I'm not straight on that trumpet player's name.
Son Leger. Son Leger. Yeah. Where did he live? Well I think he's on a prayer between St. Philip and Dumain, a barber. He's a barber.
He's there now, huh? Yeah. He's a prayer between St. Philip and Dumain. Yeah. That's right. I didn't know how to spell that Leger, that's why I asked you.
Well you've got to be on that spelling too. It's been such a long time since I've seen him.
Well anyhow, let's see, you played with that band on drums.
Yeah, and different bands with Chris, different parties. Chris used to play mostly parties on the weekdays, you know.
Who did he play for, Chris?

Well he played like the rest of the bands. He was a named band and he was good, his style of playing. He played for a lot of Italian people, Italian halls, but mostly for colored. See he wasn't particular about the way he played, as long as he was playing.
Did he play for rich people, all kinds?
All kinds, all sorts of people.
He did. What style of music did he feature, Chris?
Well you mean like the songs? Well his special song was Callous Love. That's where the wah-wah came in at. He really could do the wah-wah on the cornet. He didn't play a trumpet, he played cornet.
Was there any special reason for playing cornet?
No, I didn't know. I wouldn't know about that, why he played it, but that's what he played, the cornet.
Let me put on a record now, since you're talking about Chris. I'm going to play this, Callous Love, that came out first on the climax.
Yeah.
Can you hear it?
Yeah, I can hear it. That's the way he was starting. These men on the record.

I know they shouldn't. I guess most of the fellas in that band played with Chris at one time, aren't you? Yeah, George. That's right. I know they should. I guess most of the fellas in that band played with Chris at one time or another. Yeah, George. That's right.
Big Jim. I know they should.
I guess most of the fellas in that band played with Chris at one time or another. Yeah, George.
That's right. Big Jim.
Yeah. That's right.
Big Jim.
Would he play it like this, this boy? That's just the way he used to play. That's what the other fellows tell me too. That's right.
Oh, long years ago I used to play exactly like it.
Would he have a solo with his band?
Oh yeah, with the wah-wah. He'd take the wah-wah, most of his solos would be with that.
Would he let the clarinet play a solo like that?
Oh yeah, oh yeah.
Do you remember any bands that didn't have solos, that had ensemble all the time?
Well most all the bands that I know in my time, this man would stand out for himself.
Yeah. Would he do that little lick you just played, Chris? No, he didn't play like that.

And he'd play that solo like that. But he'd have that wah-wah with that little mute in it. Take that. Take that. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. I'm still out of tape.

Yeah. Let me turn it off before the knife comes home. So we have a pretty good idea what Chris played like from that. Yeah, that's it. Well how long were you with that first band before you went with Chris?
With Son Leger and? With Son Leger? Well quite a while. I just remember the exact time I played with them.
Would you say closer to a year, six months, two years?
Maybe about six months or something like that, or maybe a little more.
And how long were you with Chris?
Well I never was a regular man with him, but he played side jobs, you know, different kids.
I see.

And I played, after I started playing the trumpet, I played a lot of times with him. And when Sam died I'd taken his place quite a while with Izil Muggenbaum. I still moved up from second to first and I played the second.
I see. With the band. Who was Chris's regular drummer then?
Well, Roy Evans.
Roy Evans, yeah. Yeah, Roy. Roy was a wonderful drummer. Wonderful. Do you remember who would be members of Chris's band then?

Well it's about the same thing like the bands go now, they would change about it. But he had George for quite a while, and Georgia Boy, Zeb, Guy used to play the banjo mostly with him, Peter Papin, he played with him, Yank Johnson, Yank Johnson and Buddy Johnson, Yank's brother, they used to play, Earl Unford, he was his trombone player most of the time. And Chester Lazardi, bass man.
Did he use a piano ever?
I never remember Chris having a piano.
Saxophone ever? Yeah, he had saxophone.
I think Edward Gome used to play with him too. He used to play sax with him.
Which saxophone was that?
Alto sax.
He used alto more.

Alto sax and he had a fellow by the name of Pajot played, he's a barber, his name was Pajot, he used to play ten of sax with him. Well that would be mostly when they played at the Bulls Club, they'd have two or three bands every Tuesday night, where they'd have eight men's, eight or nine men's in each band.
Would they buck?
Oh yeah, that's what that was for. And they advertised every Sunday. Oh that was wonderful.
Do you remember any famous contests they had bucking like that?
Well that would go on every Tuesday over and over and over.
Who would you even do when?

Well they never would come to the conclusion. Who would win is just move from one side, in other words when this band play on this side the crowd come over and listen to that band. And when the middle band play they go inside, and the next one they go on the other side. And so it worked like that.
Would they, now let's see, that's the Elks Hall now. That's right, that's right.
Well they had a big yard on each side. See from the Elks place to Daniel Street, all that was the open space. And from that part to dry on that side, then they had the hall in the middle.
And they'd have one band in either yard?
Yeah, one on this side and one on the other side. Sometime one in the middle. Every Tuesday, that was a big night.
Why did they pick Tuesday? That's a funny day of the week.
Well at that time people used to look like, it seems to me, they went for the music more than anything and had this jukebox and so forth. And at Millenburg they had something going on every day.
What was Millenburg like?
Oh it was fine. The pavilions, they'd have some time, I imagine about six or seven bands out there.
Who would be out there at once? Do you remember who the different guys would be?
Well all the bands, Rene Band, Punchy was under the name of Kid Punchy at that time, Punchy Band, Chris Band, Jack Kerris Band, Sam Morgan Band. Kidman. All those fellas.
Sweet ones. Must have kept things jumping. Oh yeah.
That was the good old days.
Let me see. So you would substitute with Chris for Roy and take his place sometimes?

Well Chris, you know, it'd take more than one job and so forth like that and he'd go someplace and make up something and it still would be Chris' name and not have three or four jobs at that particular night.
Would he go from one to the other or stay on one?
Stay on one.
And use his name on the other thing? Yeah.
Most of the fellas used to do that. I never know if Sam would do anything like that, but most of the other fellas. Neither Pop is still a Stan.
Would people think you were Chris?

Well when I started playing trumpet, I started playing trumpet, I used to play all the favorite numbers that the people I know they'd go for and the only difference they could tell when it would come into the hall, the difference. I'd play all the numbers that he played exactly.
If they didn't know you, did they ever come up to you and say, hello Chris? No, no.

They knew who you were. After I started making a name for myself, well most of the time then after I got the band together and Chris would send me in his place on a job, well they'd sign up with me. And that's how I got real started, you know what I mean? He sent me in, I could do the same thing he was doing, I was younger and so they come to find out, they put it in there and they had more trust in me that I would come. But with the stand outside he couldn't tell the difference.
Well who else did you play with in the 20s?

Well mostly I used to always have my own band, you see. I played at the La Vida, well Jim was in charge, Jim Robinson was in charge, but I was the leader and so forth of that group. And at the Pallet Theater, well that was my group.
When were you at the La Vida? 36.
36 I was there. That's the first time it's the audition of the Social Security cards, I'll never forget that. Yeah, I got the card there in 36.
Who did you have in the band there? You had Jim as well.
Yeah, well Jim, Paul Barnes, Sidney Flusia played the guitar, Benny Turner played the piano, Robert Davis played the drum. It was six of us. That's what they said.
What did you say? You had clarinet or saxophone? Saxophone, Paul. Did he play clarinet at that time?
Yeah he could play but he didn't play the clarinet over there. He just played the saxophone.
I just wonder, because you know on the old records you hear him mostly on saxophone in the 20s?
Well yeah, when he recorded with the Pops where he played nothing but the sax.
You mean Papa Celeste? Yeah, that's right. And Jelly Roll too I think the same thing.
Yeah, when he was with Joe Oliver. He played the saxophone. I see.

Yeah so he would be more famous as a saxophone player then I guess. That's right, he would. The way you say it and everything it looks like. You must have played with somebody else in the 20s, or you say you had some other places, you had your own band.

Yeah, well I played on Bourbon Street in the 30s at 802 for Sam Columbo. It was right across from the paddock. When the paddock was open up, I had been out there playing across the street. Little Sammy Hopkins was on the piano. Charlie, what's his name? Charlie Sylvester was playing the drum. And Chester Lazard was playing the bass. And then later on we got Handy out there. I played there a long time for him. Who's Handy? John Handy, the saxophone player.
Could be other Handys too, you know. There's a many. I'm sorry, I'm sorry.
That's okay. I just said it the way I can, you should know what I'm talking about. I do know. John Handy, yeah.
I want those boys in England to know. Yeah that's right, John Handy. So he was playing saxophone. He was playing saxophone. That's right. Did you ever work with him on clarinet?

Well, no, the time when he was playing a lot of clarinet, he was the best you had here. He was working at the Humminbird on Biennale and Marie, and I was playing at a nightclub on Iberville between Marie and Villery. And like I said, most of my work at that time was of my own.
I was the leader of my band. Well what kind of clarinet was he playing then, would you call it? Was he reading or faking or what?
He was faking. He was faking, but he was great.
Did he play a lot of notes or what?
Well I wouldn't be able to explain exactly how I went, but he was really good.
Yeah, you know he's made some records, I don't know if you've ever heard of him.
No, I went over by George to listen one day and George happened not to be there. I had a chance to hear the records. With Punch I think it was.
Yeah. Tom or somebody. Punch. Yeah. I could play some tapes of him, but I'd better not. I think his lip was down when he made those records.

I'll tell you about him, he just lost interest in it. He don't like to play. That's for sure. Because when I was on Bourbon Street after some time back I had my own band at the Mardi Gras for quite a while out there for Sid. And then I played on Tuesdays with the band and I got him out there and he said it was all right until he gets on the stand and he found all kind of fault. He just don't like to play it.
Well there's very few guys who can play both alto and clarinet I notice. Well I don't know. Not too many of them can do it. I know it don't seem to bother Contrell.
He played a tenor in that. Yeah but alto I say in clarinet.
Alto.
Oh maybe so.
Maybe it's a change of key or something you know. I don't know. It seems to get him.
He just after he played so much saxophone he just played.
See there was something else I was going to ask you about your teacher. Whatever you really get into that.

Oh Professor Delmar, he was a professor, but I'd taken lessons quite a while with him. In fact most of the fellas did at that time. Where did he live? Well he had lived in a city but he was from some part of the country I just remember.
But what part of the city? Do you remember his exact account?
Well most of the time he used to be on Ramport and culminated at a pressing shop, Professor
Pritchett.
You remember that? He'd be right in there most of the time. That's where he used to be. I see.
And that's where you'd get him, huh?
Well no, he'd come to the house. He'd come to the house.
Do you remember his first name? No, I just remember that. Oh we called him first. Yeah we won't ask Pritchett.
Yeah you can ask him, he knows for sure. Professor Delmar.
That's right. And you said you had Chris at some point.
Well Chris started me off, yeah. He turned the horn and I went to him for quite a while. I started first after I'd formed the band. You see.
What did he teach you exactly? Reading?
Well reading, reading. I could read pretty close.
I didn't know whether Chris was a reader or not.
Well Chris was like the average guy it was, you might say. But some don't give a guy credit.
You know what I mean?
Some would say different things.
Would he read on the stand?

Well he didn't play no arrangement or nothing like Papa Celestan and he'd keep up with the late music. The late music mostly I'd hear him play would be maybe the introduction and the chorus of a song and like that.
So he'd talk about the sheet music then, huh?
No he would have orchestration.
Well he'd get an orchestration and just.
Well they'd have some time, they'd have good readers, would be with him like Yank, Yank was a good reader, different stuff like that. Well he'd, you know, get them together. That's right.
How long did you go to Professor Delmarine?

Well I was on and off with Chris for about five years or something, let's say something like that. Off and off. Sometimes he would leave and go out of town, go someplace in the country where he'd teach the rest of the country. And I learned a lot from Paul at the La Vida. You see, he's a good reader. Louis DeMann, he liked me, I liked him very much.
Well he was more than just a reader, didn't he?
Well he could play a few numbers or get along already a few numbers by a head, but mostly he was a reader.
Yeah but I mean he could do arrangements and everything too.
Yeah, oh yeah.
Because the Eureka played some of his stuff and the Tuxedo both. Yeah.
Well I have a lot of manuscript paper that he'd buy sheet music to keep up with all the ladies, and every time he'd get something he'd fix it and bring it down to me.
Did you ever have a real big band yourself?

Yeah, I did, most of the time. I had a lot of the fellas work with me. Bill worked a long time with me, Bill Matthews. Paggio, second trumpet. Mario Custer, played saxophone and clarinet, he's a nice trumpet player too, you know. Oh I had many of them played.
I had ten pieces.
Ten pieces.
What did Bill Matthews play then? Trombone.
Trombone. Who? Bill. No, I never, in fact, never did hear Trombone, or Bill played a drum, but I know he could.
I heard about him playing.

I used to play with his brother in the Tuxedo Brass Band, Eddie Jackson. I led the brass band, Papa Celestine and Eddie Jackson split up. I was lead man and Paggio was second, and Duran, Maurice Duran. We two was on solo.
Who else was in the band?
Oh, I just, it's kind of weird. Well the drummers you ought to know. Well the drummers was Bat Mosley and Remus Matthews, Bill's brother. Well that was the regular guy.
That's right. Who played bass drum? Oh, Bat.
And Remus played Smell.
That's right. And Eddie Jackson was in there.
Yeah, he was a tuba man. Great man.
I think that's about all of this reel. Before we get into anything new, I'll turn it off.
So this is real, too. Get out. What about in the 20s? Did you work with any brass bands

back then? Yeah, well I worked with practically all the brass bands in the 20s. Before depression? Yeah. Before 1929? I worked then, and during the depression I made practically all my living off of funerals. Who did you work with? What were the names of some of the brass bands in the 20s? Well, the original Eureka brass band. I started playing in the band with Wilson, Lita, Schatz was the second man, but after I got into the band, and Wilson taking sick, well I started leading the band. Wilson and Johnny, his brother,
it was their band. What's Wilson's first name? I didn't

get it. Oh, I know his brother was named Johnny Wilson. I just remember what his name was. His brother was Johnny Wilson, and old man Bob was playing in that band at that time. Ray, the bass player, he was playing trombone at that time. Big Connie, they were playing. I played that band, and I played with the Pacific band with Rene, with Rene was the lead, and I don't know, he quit or something. I led that band with Talbot. He was playing trumpet. And Edgar Mosley, he was playing the bass drum. I can't recall exactly all the fellas in that band. Pacific brass band. Brass band, yeah,
a brass band at that time. Did they have a clarinet player?
Yeah, they had a clarinet player. George used to play a lot of times with us in that band,
and he was playing the bass band. Let's see, alto player? Let's see, I'm trying to think of who the alto players were in that band.
In the brass band? In the Pacific. In the Pacific.
Alto horn. Manny Gabriel. Yeah. An alto saxophone? Alto saxophone. I thought maybe they had an alto horn there.
Oh. Old Man Bob used to mostly play with all the bands that Old Man Bob ran. He played alto horn. Then they had a fellow called Flowers, he used to play at the alto horn, the peck horn,

in that band too. Where was he from, Flowers? The West Indian. That you make our song. That's right. Let's see. Got to check all this. Uh. When the secretary comes, we got your name and an index here. We want to check that over. Let me see. So you played with the Pacific, Eureka?

That's right, Tuxedo, when Eddie Jackson takes over. Yeah. I played with Eureka. Who was this guy, Gassoon? Gassoon was a banjo man. I met him on my way coming up, but he had to go to the clinic. Other than that I'd have brought him over. Well who was? I mean Gassoon, his name is Joe Phillip. But did he play in the brass band? No, no, he played in the band. He played with Chris and with me, most of the time with Rene and different fellas.
Let me find something from the interview that Bill did with you. Hold on a second. When you came into the Eureka, what part did they give you?
Uh, the second part. That's the first in the brass band. I was in the middle.
I see. Well who decided about what part you should take?

Well, about the part I should have taken, it was undecided. They didn't know I could read. And Ernest Rogers played the drum. He the one that brought me in. They needed a man to play, so he recommended me, which he used to play in the brass band, in the Pacific band. And he recommended me to Wilson, so we got there, I could hear him talk, and they didn't know. This is one of them kids that's like, a kid playing, a kid somebody, or something like a kid. And so after they gave me the part and I played all right, well they take me in the band. Then they put Shot Spike on the second, put me with Wilson, and after Wilson taken sick, and I led the band for a long time. The man, he played a lot of times, solos with different fellas, Huntley Gordet. What's his name? Huntley Gordet. Huntley Gordet.
Yeah. You know what I heard of him? Somewhere. Who else did he play with?
Well, Luis the man taught him. He had his own band. He died in California somewhere.

Is that the guy that played with Jack Carey? Yeah, he played with a lot of those things. He did. He would play with the writing bands, going there? Yeah. Yeah. What about your father? Did he play music? No, nobody in the family played music at that time. Did they sing? Well yeah, but there's church members,

they sing in the church. And my daddy, well he used to dance a little, and you know that old time stuff, he used to do the buck dance and play the comb with the broom like a slide trombone with the guitar players and so forth. With the broom? Well he put the broom, you know, put on the shoulder like you do with the trombone and put a piece of paper on the comb and blow through that. You don't have a comb with you? I wish I
had one. No. Well you could demonstrate that for us. Well I mean it just, it would take the comb and

the cigarette, you know what you make cigarettes with, you put that on there and just blow through it, just like he was speaking or something. I mean, just like he was speaking. Did he feature any particular number? Well most of the songs that they sing at that time. Such as? Well I wouldn't remember what they played.
I thought maybe it's something you might remember when you were the old boy.
No, I wouldn't remember just anything. Did you ever know a drummer named Rudolph? Yeah. Who is he? Well he played with Sam quite a while too. Yeah, he played with Sam.
What does he look like? Which Rudolph is that? He's a heavy star bright fellow. That's the one who's alive now? Yeah.
Rudolph Bollier. Bollier, that's right. He's kin to Arnold De Pears.
I see. Did you play any other instruments besides trumpet and drums?
Well no, I used to fool with the guitar but I never got in the way with that.
What did you play on the guitar? Just rap the blues. Did you use a pick or fingers? Fingers.
It's too bad you can't do that today. No. Yeah, you got something there.
Yeah. If I gave you a guitar could you do it? I don't know. Well I got one here I played.
I doubt it man. I doubt it. It might hurt your hand.
Yeah. Very tender. Let's see. Who started you off on the cornet? How did you get your first instrument?

Well I got the first instrument when I was working at the carolero store on Canelo Street. They had the King Dentist next door and there was a fellow, he was trying to learn the cornet. It was the cornet when I first played. And so he asked me if I wanted to buy it. So I told him no, I was playing the drum, which I always liked the horn instrument. And so he told me, he said, let me have it for five dollars. Somebody didn't have five dollars. He said, well all right, you take the horn. And he said, once and ever you got something, you paid it five dollars. So I got the horn, the cornet, and I went to Chris with the cornet. And for the first start, the sound of the horn, he rolled a piece of paper, put my mouth like you're going to spit and just sound the horn. And he wrote the first scale, a major scale, the horn, the half, the quart, the heat, and so forth.
I see. This guy next door to you when you were in the curio shop?
Yeah.
Did he play much?
He didn't play at all. Just happened to have. He bought the horn. He pretended to play it, but he somehow or other didn't make no way with it, so he sold it to me for five dollars.
Ever know anybody named Pratt?
Yeah. That's to be Chris Wright Man, Banjo Man.
What's his full name? I just remember that.
Pratt, huh? This fellow which we call Sambo, his name is Edgar Joseph. You know him, huh? Yeah. Well that's really a relation to him. You call him and ask him, he'll tell you.
Well we'll get it from him.
Yeah, you can get it from him, sure.
What were some of the early tunes that you remember? You know, way back.

Well, my first tune, what I used to play, yes, that's my baby. And then I got saved about Chris. I played the blues by Maryland and Going Back to Jamaica. And mostly everything that Chris played that I knew that the folks was interested and liked it, I built up on that.
Now that Going Back to Jamaica is the same thing as West Indies Blues and all that. That's right.

We'll call it Going Back to Jamaica, yeah. Well that's his to feature himself with that wah-wah. See? He played a tune, open with the horn, but when he gets to his time to feature himself, well that's why he did a lot of that. And that's his main tune and my Maryland.
What's a Jitney dance?

Well a Jitney dance is where they chose one time as a Nicola to dance, they had girls awake there. Anybody who wanted to come in, most of the sailors and so forth would come in, they'd buy a string of tickets, and we'd play the song very short. In other words, I'd play the first chorus, it depends on the bottom of the song, and Paul would take it out. I'd get ready for the next one to pick up.
Only two choruses in, huh?

Yeah, make them short, then make money. Then we'd have what you call a five minute slow drag or five minutes, well that'd you get a chance to play the music or play something long. Five minute waltz or five minute fox strata, five minutes what's never made be. You see?
Well those girls, did they make out all right with that money? Well I think they got about a half or something. Oh yeah, they made out all right.
Made all right. I waked it there, then I waked at the moonlight up on St. Charles and Paul Jitney. And Paul Jitney upstairs.
Which corner is that?
That was on the Riverside, downtown side corner on St. Charles Street. Right on the corner was upstairs.
Sam Pichota has that restaurant there, and Curly's or something?

Yeah, the restaurant downstairs at that time. I don't know if it's the same people or what, but Jimmy was operating the dance hall upstairs. Yeah, that's how that went to George. They'd buy a string of tickets.
Did you make any records in the twenties that weren't put out or anything?

Well we did. I mean when I was at Sam Colombo, they had a fellow who had a machine, a tape machine, I think it was, and we just got together, he'd come by your house or sofa like that, and we made records. But I don't know what I much did with it. Probably just for ourselves, you know what I mean?
This one must have been later though if it was a tape machine.
Well I had some kind of a box that we could go someplace and buy the record, the blank, you know, and we'd record what I did away with, you know, when I raised it here.
That's too bad.
I'm telling you, it was real good.
What did you record? What tunes? Do you remember?

Well, Mahogany Hall Stump, and I know for sure that Mahogany Hall Stump in China Time, all that kind of numbers. I was pretty much playing all of Louis's numbers, he put it out, when you're smiling and so
forth, all that.
When did you first meet Louis, speaking about him? The first time I met Louis to know him was in 1929 in Chicago at the Warwick Hall.
What were you doing up there?
Playing, I used to play the executions out here. The first executions I played out here was on the LNN. And the rest of them, it was 1928. The rest I went up Illinois Central.
Where did the LNN go?

Well she passed through Mobile in those places. She went to Chicago. I see. But you went around like? I went around, yeah, to Birmingham and all those places. It was the longest route, the long route.
Oh yeah. How did the people like you in Chicago?
It was all right. It wasn't that very long. It took eight days for the whole trip. But that's where we would play at, we would have to dance there.
At the Warwick Hall. At the Warwick Hall. Where was Louie?

Well, Louie came over and visited. He knew old man Joe Howard at that time. Old man Joe Howard made that first trip with me, playing the bass. And Louie came over to see him. And Percy, he was there too, Percy. Edwin Washington. Oh, it could be an Edwin.
What was Percy playing? Second trumpet. Percy Humphrey. Percy Humphrey.
Second trumpet.
He was a drummer too when he began, come to think of it. Yeah, he told me.
Oh, I never knew him to play drum. He could have been.
What did Percy do up there? He did all right.
People like him? Oh yeah, it was all right.
How big a band did you have at that time? Eight. Eight, huh? Two trumpets? Two trumpets, two saxes.

Two saxes, two trumpets, bass, drum, banjo, and I don't remember the trombone. I know one time we got a trombone player over there called Hemp. He was an old time musician from here and we got him. But he wouldn't carry no piano. Because mostly I was playing with people in the baggage called Going and Coming. While the train was rolling? No, no, when she'd make stops. Like she'd stop Memphis, Jackson, different places where she'd be over for half an hour or so.
That's where we played. With the people that? Dance, yeah. What else would they do? Have fun.
Having a little drink and stuff. Oh yeah, plenty of drinks. Did they gamble or anything?
No. They didn't gamble. Let's see, you know, I'm not going to play a game. I see, you said you had Edmund Washington, huh? That's Big Fat Wash?

Yeah, Big Wash, Henry Hardin, Tanner Sacks, and old man Joe Howard on that first trip. Joe Phillip, one you call Garsoon, he's playing the banjo. And, uh, Bat Mosley. Was on a drum. Did you ever know Guy Kelly? I'm the one who brought Guy Kelly to Chicago. How's that?
Well, uh, he wanted to go and his mother, his people, was in Chicago.

And, uh, I take them with me. In other words, because they'd hate him with me, he just played when he wanted to, he wanted to make those stops. And that's the last I seen him. He died after that. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. He went on up there, huh? Yeah.
He went there. He joined, went up there, and joined some band or another up there.
He was a great trumpet man.
What about Eddie Johnson? Did you know him?
Yeah. He made trips with me, a couple of trips with me to Chicago, and out to the Stacks.
Which one is he? Which Eddie Johnson?
The one with Wicked Weir lines? Big head.
Big head.
Big head, that's it. You know everything.
Yeah, but I know there's more than one Eddie Johnson.
Well yeah, they had the little Eddie, the bright one, he used to play saxophone too, some
time back. Were there any other New Orleans guys up there other than Louie?
Well I saw Punch when I was up there, Punch Miller. Yeah.
In fact I didn't get around.
Did you know Lee Collins down here? Oh yeah. I know Lee used to play out there at the La Vida before I did. Lee played there a long time. Yeah I know Lee a long, long time ago.
Down here, huh? Yeah. Did you ever know him in Chicago? Ever seen him out there?
Well no, I didn't ever meet him in Chicago. I knew him from here. Yeah, I did meet him in Chicago.
I think that back.
There were two executions that went to Chicago.
I was on the I.C. and he was on the LNN, and that's the time when we had that Buckingham Contest on 47th Street, 47th Avenue.
I know the Regals, it's right around the corner, Michigan Avenue I think it is, right on the corner. We tied up there for hours. That's right.
Who did Lee have with him?

Have a pretty good band? Oh yeah, yeah, good one. Yeah, George Washington on trombone, Pedro Poenelle on alto, David Jones on tenor-sikes, Daniel Parker on guitar, he had Albert Morgan on bass, and I think it was Roy on the drums though. I don't remember the drum player, but he had a good band. Regular New Orleans? Yeah, and he had the Joe Robichaud.
Regular New Orleans band though up there, huh?
Yeah, we had the, just like we used to do it here on the streets, we did it over there.
I see. Who played the slide whistle around here? That little Frisco whistle? Played a slide? Slide whistle? You know one of those whistles you love? Frisco whistle?
Well we called him Chani Bebe, used to play with Celeste. I used to play it too, that slide whistle like that.
What was your feature on? What kind of?
Almost any song.
Did the people like it?
Well it seems to be like, yeah, it was pretty good.
I wonder why that died out, you know? I wouldn't know. What's funny. It's funny. He used to do that all the time, the bands.
That's right, Black Benny used to play with Chris too. You heard of Black Benny. He was a right hand man.

And he played? He was a good drummer. And he played, did he play the slide whistle too? I don't remember him playing the slide whistle. But he played with Chris, yeah. Did you ever work with Black Benny?
No, I didn't work with Chani Bebe.
I thought he'd be in the street or something.
No, no. I think before I got started, he passed.
What about this fellow Hickman?
Oh, he used to play saxophone, he used to play with Rene.
Alto Oteno was? Alto. What was his first name, do you know? Maybe that was his first name, I don't know. I forgot. His first name, yeah. Did he ever play with you much?

Not that much. We played quite a bit at the White Place, which he was leading up to play off the normal and advertised for Maison Blancenic. He had that job in charge. But he sticked with Rene for a long time.
Who was in the Meilenburg job with Hickman? Who else?
Louie Gallo, myself, on trumpet, and I think it was Albert George who played a drummer. That was what was Forrest was.
What did Gallo play then?
Piano.
They had pianos out there on the lake, huh? Oh yeah. I don't see how they ever moved them out there on those flanks.
They were out there.
They had them out there. Gosh, yeah.
Not on the pavilion, I mean this was on land.
Oh I see, out near the. Yeah, it was right out there, but on land. What was the name of the place? Got me there.
Been too long ago.
Did you ever work with Burbank?

Burbank worked with me. Yeah? Where? He played a lot of jobs with me off and on, and we played together for Maison Blanche, Annex. Well it was, he got the job, but most of the time he couldn't play, well I used to take the band over.
For Maison Blanche, Annex?

Yeah, they used to advertise once or twice every week. Instead of the papers what they had in the TV, we'd get on the street. We'd take uptown route in the morning, twelve o'clock we'd take a break for an hour, then we'd wake downtown in the afternoon.
That was on a truck?
About five years.
What makes a good jazz musician anyhow? I could figure that out.

Well it's just about the way I can figure it would make him good. It's something that he wants to do, and he just let go with it. Well do you think the reading helps? Well I don't, I wouldn't know exactly, but the reading would help him to play. They got some fellas to read, and that's but all, they don't have nothing with it. You know what I mean? But to my idea, the guy playing something, the way he feels he should play it, it should come out better.
Do you have any special tricks, you know, to make you play jazz better? Any kind of special way of playing your instrument?
No, I don't know, special way that I have noticed to make me, other than when I used to drink, well, some time I didn't feel like playing and get a taste, so well, that would change things.
Do you lip your horn in a special way?
Well, no, I put the pressure most on the top lip, right here.
I just wondered, I noticed some guy seemed to sort of turn their lip out.
Oh no, no, no.
And you just lip it regularly.
I put it regularly there, right at the center, here and there. I'm trying to remember who used to do that.
It might have been Kit Clayton or something.
Yeah, Clayton would play most with the mouthpiece down in the bottom lip.
Inside the bottom lip? Yeah. That's a funny way of playing. I know that I understand. Well it is.
I mean, Pop used to blow on the side, well on the side. Yeah, Celestine.
Yeah. Remember that, he looked funny. His mouth was all screwed around and everything.
He tells you, I mean the book tells you the proper way to play it, but then if you can't get it in any way it's comfortable to you, that's the way it goes.
Who were some of your favorite trumpet players when you were growing up other than Chris? Well I liked it all.
I liked the punch, I liked the Rene, all of them had different styles, Sam. I liked them all. I just liked the music, period. Yeah.
What kind of music did Sam feature?

Well he was more on the sweet side. He played, he had this old fish head and all of them. He had a kind of, the most solid beat with his music, you know what I mean? And sweet. He wasn't rough. He wasn't a rough trumpet player.
Did he play in the thunks?

Well I never knew him to play in the thunks. I know mostly he used to travel on the coast. He was a big name for that at that time. He was great. Nobody, when he was in town and in places like that, that was it. People flocked to him. He used to play on the Astoria. He'd be packaging all the time. But mostly his playing was out of town.
Have you ever heard any of the Sam Morgan records?
Yeah I heard his records sing on and everybody talking about Sam, yeah.
Did he sound like that in person? Yeah. The records did him justice in it.
Yeah that's the way it sounded.
Sweet like that. Yeah. Who were the loud trumpet players in there, the real blasters in those times?
Well I know Manny Perez was a loud, loud man. He blastered a lot.
Did he play any jazz? All in his way.

But at that time when I, before I started playing the music, those bands, manual bands and so forth like that, they didn't play this kind of stuff like we do on the street. No, you know. They played marches at all times. Everything that they played was by the paper. See, they go to get the body marches, fuel marches, and they leave, marches again.
Well did they have any real trunk brass bands?
Well at that time I didn't know of any other than no. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .
We were talking about those brass bands. You were saying Chris would get together, some of those guys?

Well yeah, bands like Renee and Chris, I mean our leaders like Renee and Chris, well they'd get a band, well then they would play this rough stuff like we do today, going and coming back to him to go to pick up the body, and what we call put them in the alley coming back. Put them in the alley? What does that mean? It's the blues. You know what I mean. I know what you mean.
I'm telling you the blues.
And I want you to tell me. The blues, man. But why did you call it put them in the alley? Well I just, I found it going on in the back.
I was at the gutter to pick up the body, and what we call put them in the alley coming back.
I guess you might wake up in the alley sometimes.
Well I haven't so far. You never woke up and didn't know where you're at?
I never did get that much. No.
Well say a funeral like Buddy Petit's funeral, who would play that?
I had a get together band, and Eureka played two bands. Louis Armstrong was part there. That's the time he was here at the Suburban Garden.
Do you remember who you had in your band?

All I could remember now, for sure, I know Jim was there, Big Jim, Robinson, and Edgar Mosley, the drum. That's but all I could remember. It's been such a long time ago. Well who paid you for that? Well we had the speakeasy at that time. You know what I mean by speakeasy. Well they had speakeasy, and the guy that operated the speakeasy, he paid for it. Because we left from his place, and we came back to his place, and brought the crowd.
Well he might have made money on that deal. Well he did. Was he a friend of Buddy's or something? No he was a friend of mine. He put up the money, huh? Oh yeah.
I used to play a lot of dancing for him at Poisevere and Hall of Economy, Incorporated, and so forth. What was his name? Ernest Delaro. He died some time back in Chicago.
Does his family play music any of them? No he wasn't a musician.
He just operated his business.
I thought I knew some Delaroes that played music.
Yeah, the brothers that have the shoemaker shop on Claver. That's right. Played saxophone clarinet.
See? How many people came to Buddy's funeral?
Well I don't know. It was something like the funeral was something on the order of Bicu you might say. Not quite as many, but he was well known.
Well did you know a guy named Hamp Vinson?
Hamp Vinson, yeah. That was the guy I was trying to call about in Chicago, Hamp Vinson. He the one who played trombone some time with us over there.
Yeah, that's the fella.
I couldn't think of the name. Yeah. Yeah, Hamp Vinson.
Why don't we get Anders over here, and we can talk about Europe for a while. He can maybe question you about Europe better than I can. Oh, I see.
He's going to do the interview.
He's going to do the interview. And I'll watch the machine. Just sit down there and you can ask him about Europe.
Want me to start right now? Yeah, anytime.
Oh, you want to? No, just ask him about Europe, not just Denmark but England too. Anything you know about over there.
When was your first chance to go to Europe?
Well the time that I came with George, that's my first chance to go with George Lewis.
Jazz band. Jazz band, yeah. You saw quite a few of the European countries, didn't you?
Oh, I saw a great deal of them.
Playing in England for a long time?
Well we played in England about three or four weeks.
And which other countries do you remember the name of them?
Well, I'll never forget Denmark, that's for sure, in Sweden. And you went to Germany too, didn't you?
Yeah, that was close. I think you made about, as far as I remember, you made about ten concerts in Germany, didn't you?
Well, no, we didn't do concerts.
We did a television show. Oh yeah, that's right. You just made it to a, George stayed a little after you left.
Well yeah, George, yeah, he joined up with Kent's band.
Yeah, that's right. And then he toured alone. That's right.
Who's Kent? Which one is it? Kent Collier.
Kent Collier, the British trumpet player. Yeah, that's right. So you played both in concerts and television, clubs as far as I remember?
Yeah, we played mostly concerts. Yeah. But when we went to Germany, well we did mostly rehearsing for about four or five days for the show.
Was that your first television experience? Oh no. You've been doing television before?
The television here, New York and Los Angeles and San Francisco.
Was it very different to do television in Europe?
No, it was okay. It was okay. It was one thing, but like all the stations, the lights, it was tough.
I'm sure that Dick would like to know a little about how you find the European audience compared to the American audience, especially the audience here in New Orleans.
Well, they were wonderful, wonderful audiences.
You think they understand anything?

Well, I'm quite sure they did. They made sure that they were very quiet until things was, you do a number, they'll wait completely, until everything was over before they would applaud and let you know that they enjoyed.

Yeah. Yeah. Well, I think the European audience seems to me to be very serious about jazz music, but maybe it's interesting to go into the shop a little further. Did you have the feeling that they understood the background of the music, that they, did they applaud in the right places when you were playing nice and good?
Oh yeah, you could tell when they, you get to feel that feeling on them, you could tell, you could feel them.
Did you have a chance to listen to any of the European jazz bands?

Well, frankly all of them, because we were, we were to all the nice spots. The first one that we went to, when we arrived in Liverpool, we had to stay overnight, and I, I got kind of unconcerned about going on the ground. I had double band, this is what's thing is that, you know. And we've had a good many good musicians over there that night, we had a jam section.
They all wanted you to come and play with the band. Yeah, we did. We did.
In fact, every place we went. You enjoyed it?
We enjoyed it.
We enjoyed it. After the concert we would go down and join it with them and have a wonderful time.
What's the main difference, do you think, between the way the kids in Europe play your music and the way you play right here in New Orleans?

Well to my idea it's real good. That's all I could say about it. They play the tunes wonderfully and they play the same tune that we play. And in fact when we got to, when we arrived in London, the brass band, when we were getting off the train and I heard the brass band I couldn't believe my ears. They were playing the same, the song that we play is on the street and it was good.
I remember there was a brass band down receiving you almost in every city or right? Yeah, that's right.
The smallest group was the three pieces if you remember in Sweden and they still was out, the young fellow. I think it was saxophone, banjo, or something else. But anyway that was the smallest band.
In the morning you arrived at Copenhagen I think that was, you missed some train or something happened going to.

Well we came to Copenhagen but we couldn't come down due to the weather. So we had to go back into Hamsburg in Germany and we got the night train out and we arrived in Copenhagen that Sunday morning. At 6 o'clock.
Yeah. In the morning. And right away you had to go down and play I think in the entrance hall.
What about coming into London? I wanted to ask you what happened after, when you arrived in the train station in London.

Oh that's what I was speaking about. Kent's band, he had about a twenty piece brass band or something like that. And the song that they were playing sounded the same like the way we played. And they had people on top of the sheds and so forth. And I understood that a couple of them got away to, been caved in.
Well they had some people there. They did have some people. She said hey. Go ahead. I just want to know about that, that came in.
I see. Did you have an opportunity to, besides meeting the European musicians, to meet European fans of jazz and talk to them about the, do you feel they were very interested in the music?
Well yeah, we had quite a bit of people would come during the day and come up and talk.
Yeah.
About the, and we was interviewed quite a bit in London by reporters and so forth.
They wanted to get the message from you. Yeah. The message from you. That's right. Would you like to go to Europe again?
I should say I would.
Did you miss New Orleans very much?

No, I'm afraid I didn't. At first I did because at that time when we was, came back to Liverpool when we was making a tour all over Europe. We came back to London when I was to water up at my daughter. That's right. And the night on the stage we was doing a concert, we got a telegram that she had a little baby girl and after that everything was fine.
Everything was fine.
Yeah, but love said it all about that.
I see.
And after that, well.

I've noticed that in corresponding with different musicians here in New Orleans, I asked them if they would like to go to Europe on tour because I know that sometimes there has maybe more work to be found there than there is around here at the moment, that they don't seem to be too keen on leaving the city here.
Oh, yeah.
And they're just a little scared of what might be ahead of them when they... Well, I don't see why they should. Do you think it's because they don't know so much about Europe? They don't...
Well, probably they haven't talked to the right people. Those that I talked to, I explained to them the best I knew and tell them exactly the absolute thanks. Yeah.
Do you find it hard and tiring to work in those concerts in Europe? It's always very big halls and...

Well, no, because you get your breaks. Well, the only thing, well, you'd expect that, is when you get the breaks you have the autographs and this and talk to that one or two at that time, and you're supposed to get a rest, which you don't. You know. That's in the game. Did you know that New Orleans jazz was so popular in Europe? I didn't. And that people really started it then? I was surprised when I heard the fellas play so wonderful.
Most of the people knew your name? Yeah, they did. That fellow John Selter. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. He's a young trumpet player. Mm-hm. And he plays exactly like I played.
He surprised me .
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Well you know some of the old Ken Collier things sound a lot like it too. Willenberg-Joy, I remember he'd play a lot of your breaks and everything.
Did you meet Ken Collier when he was?
Oh yeah, we had a fine time at his home.
Until he? Yeah, he put on a real fine time.
And we used to go down where he was playing every night.
The nights we'd be off, we'd be right over there jamming with him. You knew him here from New Orleans when he was there?
Yeah, I knew him from here. When he came down here.
We used to follow him in parades and funerals I guess down here, didn't we?
Yeah. He played a lot. He had up to us playing. Here?
Yeah, he played. He played down here but we'd go and be in the second line following the parades and stuff
you see.
That's right.
That's right.
Who was this guy who had you on television in Germany?
Oh, I just remember the name, George. You know he was head of that and Sideman, all that dude would play. Probably called him Joe.
His name is Jace Berend. Joe Berend. Yes. Joe Berend. Yes.
Joe Berend, yes.
I think that was the name. It was nice there too. In fact, everyone.
He's been back here you know, he might come back again.
Yeah.
What club did you play in in Denmark, did you tell?
Well you have to ask him. I know that we had so much time, I had time to look for the name of the place, I would ask for the name of the place every night.

Well actually the whole band did a concert in Copenhagen's largest hall, the KB Hall, which was very successful. It was so successful as a matter of fact that even though George planned to go back to the States after the Copenhagen venues, we talked him into staying and opening a new club that was there, the Montmartre Club. You opened the Montmartre Club, George did? Yeah, George opened it. The first band in there. The very first band in there. And I think that I've never seen so many people in my life, it was hard to get the musicians in there. And there was hundreds and hundreds of people standing outside waiting all night to get there. It was very, very crowded. We all had, at that time the dressing room wasn't finished yet, and we all had to stand in the kitchen during the intervals. Yeah, that's right. We had some beers and some fun out there. It was hard to cook though. You didn't get much of a chance to cook.
Well what band has drawn the best in Copenhagen of all the bands you've had in the Montmartre?

George's band, in the Montmartre, if you want to refer to that particular place. Yeah, that particular place. Yes. I mean George's band was outstanding. I haven't seen anything like it in the traditional field. Speaking about progressive and modern jazz, when Stan Getz and Moe's Allison opened the club, just after George and the band were there, there was a lot of people too.
So would you say Stan Getz and Moe's Allison at Drew George?

Well that's very hard to say because George was there for about I think eight or ten days in total, you know. And that was full, the club was full, very, every night. And Stan was there for almost a year. And the first eight days was very full naturally as it would be. And then it balanced out so that it was Friday, Saturday and Sunday was very full. And Copenhagen is a city of about a million people or something like that. And there's just a natural demand for jazz. And they stayed so long. Sure should have liked to have George playing there. But he came back and played there later on the second term.
So then George Louis Armstrong is about as well as anybody in Europe then, roughly.

I would say so. I mean Louis Armstrong is, I mean Louis Armstrong takes in a lot of people that are not particularly interested in jazz but because of the outstanding amount of publicity he gets and because he also plays humorous versions of numbers that are well known to a lot of old timers because you might realize that in Europe it's the young people that go for jazz, college students and all the young boys and girls. And Louis Armstrong was just the first band to come over and make a success out of jazz in Europe and he'll never be forgotten for that. So I mean he's a top drawer.
He draws better than George Louis.

He draws better than anybody. I mean he draws better than most classical singers or anything. I think he made ten concerts in the KB Hall last time he was there and that holds about four thousand people and that means that forty thousand people out of Copenhagen came to see him, you know. And that was just a year after he was there last time and it goes like that every time between forty and sixty thousand people and that's outstanding. I don't think there's a single entertainer in the whole world that can do that. And then it's not important what group Louis brings, you know.
